title: Eliminate the channel: volatile Ag/Ag2S gap-type atomic switch access
idea: Use a gap-type atomic switch: a 1-2 nm vacuum gap between an Ag2S electrode and a Pt counter electrode, where a gate pulse grows a single-atom Ag bridge for access and the bridge dissolves spontaneously when bias is removed. The off state is a true vacuum gap with tunnel leakage below 1e-20 A.
why: Retention set only by capacitor dielectric, so refresh is eliminated; built with e-beam lithography and evaporation in any university fab; endurance and speed are open risks.

title: Minify the flush: dirty-line tracking plus deep-trench energy bank
idea: Each DRAM bank tracks dirty rows in a bitmap and keeps an on-die deep-trench capacitor bank sized only to flush the dirty fraction into a co-integrated MRAM shadow subarray at power loss; clean rows are already mirrored in NV storage.
why: Persistence with no supercaps or batteries: hold-up energy 10-100x smaller; DRAM speed and endurance kept, NV wear only from dirty data.

title: Photoconductive access switch opened by waveguide light pulses
idea: Po: the switch is opened by light. Replace the access transistor with an a-Si:H or chalcogenide photoconductor between bitline and storage node; the wordline is a silicon-nitride waveguide, and a light pulse makes the row conductive for nanoseconds, while in the dark leakage is bulk dark current (aA) with no gate, no GIDL and no wordline voltage.
why: Facts 3 and 10: no 3 V wordline and no GIDL, with dark-current-limited leakage allowing minute-scale refresh; risk is photoconductor speed and optical power per row.

title: Diamond inversion-channel access transistor with week-long retention
idea: C: build the access device as an inversion-channel diamond MOSFET (phosphorus-doped n-type diamond with an Al2O3 gate, p-channel inversion) grown as diamond-on-Si; the 5.5 eV gap makes intrinsic carrier density ~10^-27 cm^-3, so off-current is set only by defects and storage nodes could hold charge for days.
why: Removes refresh (fact 3) and frees capacitor margin so Cs can shrink (fact 1); retention margin ~10^5x larger, with cost hinging on heteroepitaxial diamond quality.

title: Single-electron memory variability averaged out by printed Au55 cluster arrays
idea: Single-electron memories died because random background charges shifted each Coulomb-blockade island's threshold. Print a dense monolayer of ligand-capped ~1.4 nm gold clusters between storage node and bitline. Thousands of junctions in series and parallel average out the offset charges, and the room-temperature blockade (~0.2-0.3 eV charging energy) blocks conduction below threshold.
why: A printable two-terminal access element with exponential sub-threshold suppression and no semiconductor generation current, a new leakage physics. Speculative.

title: Wordline-gated Coulomb-blockade nanodot valve in storage-node contact
idea: Effect: Coulomb blockade. A ~1 nm Pt or Si nanodot between two tunnel barriers sits in the storage-node plug, capacitively gated by the same wordline: wordline-high moves the dot to its charge-degeneracy point (conducts), wordline-low leaves it deep in blockade with charging energy ~0.6 eV, above the 0.5 V node-to-bitline hold bias, so it blocks transistor leakage in series. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): claims 10x retention used for die-internal refresh skipping behind standard REF. Risk: on-current through dots vs tRCD/tWR (needs parallel dots).

title: Mechanosensitive-channel piezo-strain gated access switch
idea: Bacterial MscL opens only when membrane tension stretches it; build the access switch from a pressure-driven insulator-to-metal piezoresistor (SmSe or Cr-doped V2O3 film) squeezed by a ScAlN piezoelectric wordline actuator, so the channel is a true band insulator until the wordline strains it metallic.
why: Off-current is limited by insulator conduction, not the Boltzmann subthreshold tail (~1e-20 A), and piezo gain can let the wordline swing <1 V instead of ~3 V, cutting wordline CV2 energy ~9x.

title: Eliminate charged cells: inversion encoding plus refresh skip for discharged rows
idea: Each row stores a 1-bit inversion flag chosen at write time so most cells sit in the discharged, non-leaking state; rows whose cells are all discharged (zero pages, sparse activations, quantized weights' high bits) are flagged and skipped by refresh.
why: AI tensors are 30-70% zero or sparse; skipping such rows and halving charged cells elsewhere cuts refresh count 30-50% and lowers row-hammer exposure (fact 9).

title: Leak-direction encoding stores most cells in the discharged state
idea: Worse: store data so many cells hold leaky charge. Flip: a per-64-bit invert flag picks the polarity that maximizes cells in the non-leaking state (true or anti cell aware); rows whose vulnerable-cell count stays below an ECC-covered threshold get 4x longer refresh.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) down 2-4x for ~1.5% capacity overhead.

title: Ephemeral RAM: leaky poly-Si cells for data that dies young
idea: IFR: the data dies before the bit does. Define an ephemeral memory class with 0.5-2 ms retention made of cheap, leaky poly-Si 2T0C gain cells stacked in NAND-style tiers, and have the accelerator runtime map only activations, gradients and KV blocks with measured lifetimes under a millisecond onto it, so refresh is never issued.
why: Constraint: accepting poor leakage buys NAND-like stacking cost, >10x density at about the same wafer cost, with zero refresh for the large short-lived share of accelerator traffic.

title: ZnON back-end access tier stacked over the periphery
idea: Scale shift from front-end silicon to the back end of line: build access transistors in zinc oxynitride (Zn, O, N; no In or Ga) at <=400 C directly above the CMOS sense amplifiers and stack 4-8 tiers; the wide bandgap and absence of hole conduction give ~1e-18 A/um off-current while ~50-100 cm^2/Vs mobility keeps ns access.
why: Periphery area (fact 7, 49% of die) is reclaimed by building the array over it, and leakage (fact 3) falls so refresh stretches to seconds, without IGZO's In/Ga chokepoints.

title: Thin the die, bias its back: backside retention-bias retrofit
idea: 10-person constraint: post-process purchased dies rather than run a fab. Thin commodity DRAM dies to ~20 um, deposit a backside contact, and add a package bond that applies negative substrate bias in standby. In processes where the array well couples to the substrate, the body effect raises access-transistor Vt and lowers standby leakage.
why: Fact 3: a 200-300 mV Vt rise gives ~10-100x less subthreshold leakage and far fewer self-refreshes. Risk: triple-well isolation may block the coupling, so each vendor's part needs a teardown first.

title: Club bouncer's guest list: cold-source energy-filter access FET
idea: A bouncer admits only the guests on the list. The access transistor gets a 'cold source': a semimetal or superlattice source whose density of states cuts off above a narrow energy window, filtering out the hot Boltzmann-tail electrons behind subthreshold leakage, so slope reaches ~30-40 mV/dec at room temperature.
why: Same leakage at ~0.4 V lower threshold lets a ~1 V wordline run without a pump, ~10-15x lower wordline energy per access, with no ferroelectric or moving parts.

title: Ephemeral DRAM tier sold from retention-failing dies
idea: Worse: scrap every die that misses 64 ms retention. Flip: bin 4-16 ms dies as refresh-free 'ephemeral memory' for AI activations and KV tiles overwritten every few ms, with the controller guaranteeing rewrite-before-expiry or recompute.
why: Raises usable bit supply 5-15% from existing wafers and removes refresh for that tier (scarcity, fact 3).

title: Hydrogen-split layer transfer stacks single-crystal silicon tiers for 3D DRAM
idea: H: for each tier, bond a hydrogen-implanted donor wafer onto the finished lower tier below 400 C and cleave at the implant plane (Smart-Cut), leaving a ~30 nm single-crystal Si film in which DUV-patterned lateral access transistors are built; donors are reused ~10x, so density comes from tiers, not EUV shrink.
why: Single-crystal channels give silicon-grade low leakage in every 3D tier (facts 2, 3) with zero EUV layers (fact 4); each tier costs a bond-and-cleave instead of a litho node.

title: Downhole-grade amorphous Ga2O3 BEOL access transistor
idea: Oil-well electronics survive 200 C with wide-bandgap channels; deposit an amorphous Ga2O3 channel (4.8 eV gap vs IGZO ~3.2 eV) below 400 C as a vertical BEOL access device over the capacitor array. Generation leakage scales roughly as exp(-Eg/2kT), so off-current at 85 C should sit orders of magnitude below IGZO and silicon.
why: Facts 2 and 3: retention of minutes even when hot, so refresh nearly disappears, and the access device moves to low-temperature deposition that stacks in 3D; risk is low mobility (~1-10 cm2/Vs) and contact resistance.

title: 4H-SiC access-transistor arrays built in U.S. SiC power fabs
idea: Worse at 125 C: use silicon, whose intrinsic carrier density explodes with temperature. Flip: build the access transistor and a trench capacitor in 4H-SiC (n_i ~1e-5 cm^-3 at 125 C versus ~1e12 for Si) using under-used U.S. SiC power-device fab tooling, bonded to a Si periphery wafer.
why: Generation leakage effectively eliminated, giving minutes-to-hours retention at 125 C (fact 3), on non-EUV U.S. lines (fact 4, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Thermal-map data placement keeps long-lived data in coolest banks
idea: Worse at 125 C: place long-lived data next to the hot spot and refresh the whole die for the hottest bank. Flip: per-bank on-die thermal sensors feed the controller, which migrates rarely written pages to edge banks 10-15 C cooler and refreshes each bank at its own temperature-indexed rate.
why: Hot refresh energy (fact 3) down 2-3x on automotive and edge modules.

title: Coin collector counts every coin: few-electron Coulomb-blockade cells
idea: A coin collector tracks each coin. Each bit is ~50-200 electrons on a 5 nm silicon or metal nanodot, reached through Coulomb-blockade tunnel junctions of a single-electron access transistor; the island charging energy (>10 kT) blocks leakage, and a ~0.3 V gate swing moves the electrons.
why: Charge per bit drops ~100x from ~30k electrons, and swing to ~0.3 V, so device-level access energy falls ~100x; revisits Hitachi's PLED concept with modern nanodot precision.

title: Child's empty cups: minority-charge encoding with zero-row refresh skip
idea: A child notes that empty cups cannot spill. Each 64-bit word is stored with one invert bit chosen so at most half its cells sit in the charged (leak-prone) state, respecting true-cell/anti-cell polarity; a per-row 'all-safe' flag set on write lets the refresh engine skip rows that hold only discharged states.
why: Retention failures come only from charged cells: halving them halves tail exposure, and zero-filled or sparse rows (often 20-40% of server pages) skip refresh entirely; ~1.5-2.5x refresh energy cut for ~1.6% storage overhead.

title: Purdue GaAs heterojunction storage well revived on silicon
idea: Revive the 1980s-90s Purdue AlGaAs/GaAs DRAM cells, which held charge for hours at room temperature because electrons sat in a well bounded by a wide-gap barrier: integrate a selectively grown heterostructure storage well (AlGaAs/GaAs, or GaP/AlP, which is lattice-closer to Si) on silicon, so stored charge can escape only by thermionic emission over 0.4-1 eV band offsets.
why: Storage-node leakage is set by the band offset rather than by junction or trap generation (fact 3); retention orders of magnitude longer would make refresh rare.

title: TCP congestion control applied to the refresh interval
idea: Adapted from TCP's additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease loop: each bank's refresh interval grows a step every epoch while patrol scrubs see zero ECC-corrected retention errors, and halves as soon as one appears, with a hard floor at JEDEC timing. Corrected errors play the role of packet loss.
why: Finds each part's real retention limit at its real temperature and age instead of the worst-case spec, typically 4-8x longer intervals in cool, lightly loaded systems (fact 3), with no new cell physics.

title: Move drain high-field region into wide-gap heterojunction contact
idea: Substitute the n+ Si storage-node junction with a heterojunction: the gate-drain overlap and storage contact are n+ ZnO or TiO2 (Eg ~3.3 eV) grown on the Si channel. The conduction bands align so electrons pass, while a ~2-3 eV valence offset blocks holes. The high-field region where GIDL and SRH generation occur now sits in a material with ~1e-20 lower intrinsic carrier density.
why: Leakage tail (GIDL + junction): targets a 10-100x drop in the <=13 fA tail, extending tREF by 10x or more and cutting refresh energy ~90%.

title: Cold-source access transistor halves wordline voltage
idea: IFR: a switch that turns off infinitely sharply. Put a semimetal or graphene cold source on the bitline side of a vertical access transistor so injected carriers have a truncated thermal tail, giving ~30-40 mV/dec; the same on/off ratio then needs about half the gate swing.
why: Facts 3 and 10: VPP drops from ~3 V to ~1.5 V for ~4x less wordline CV^2 and smaller charge pumps, or at the same VPP the leakage tail drops ~100x and refresh becomes rare.

title: Octopus's arm brains: 3D latch sense amps on 8-cell bitlines
idea: An octopus puts neurons in every arm. A back-end oxide-semiconductor latch sense amp is stacked above every 8-cell vertical bitline segment, so a cell shares charge with ~0.2 fF instead of a ~60 fF, 512-cell bitline, and only a gated global line carries the result out.
why: Bitline charging dominates array energy; cutting bitline load ~100x allows a 0.5 V array with large signals, ~10x lower energy per access, and moves sense amps off the substrate (periphery is ~49% of die, fact 7).

title: Lattice-matched GaP storage-node junction starves GIDL and SRH generation
idea: Silicon's 1.12 eV gap is what makes band-to-band tunneling at the gate-drain overlap easy. Regrow only the storage-node contact as 5-10 nm n+ GaP (2.26 eV, 0.37% lattice mismatch to Si) by selective MOCVD. The high-field overlap and the metallurgical junction then lie in wide-gap material, while the channel stays silicon for drive current.
why: BTBT rate ~ exp(-B*Eg^1.5/F), so doubling Eg multiplies the exponent about 2.9x and cuts GIDL by >1e5 at equal field. SRH generation in the GaP volume falls ~1e9 through n_i. Together they attack the GIDL/TAT-dominated 13 fA tail for an estimated 4-10x longer refresh interval (fact 3).

title: Silicon-carbide 1T1C DRAM with hours-long native retention
idea: TRIZ #35 Parameter change (bandgap): build 1T1C cells on 4H-SiC wafers (Eg 3.26 eV, intrinsic carrier density ~1e18x lower than Si), where 1990s SiC DRAM test cells already showed hours-to-years room-temperature retention. A buried-channel SiC MOS access device at relaxed 40-90 nm rules serves as a refresh-free capacity tier.
why: Refresh eliminated (Fact 3); SiC boules grow by sublimation, sidestepping Spruce Pine quartz crucibles; existing U.S. SiC wafer capacity improves domestic manufacturability. Density is lower, so it targets capacity/standby tiers.

title: Lossy NUMA node standard: OS pages tagged by error tolerance
idea: Push a JEDEC/CXL descriptor that publishes each region's raw-BER-vs-refresh curve, plus a Linux 'lossy NUMA node' reached with mmap(MAP_LOSSY). KV caches, media buffers and caches go to 1%-BER regions refreshed rarely; kernel and databases stay on fully protected memory.
why: Supply and fact 3: makes 1%-BER memory a standard, procurable class so the other tolerance tricks deploy across vendors; government AI-cluster procurement can require support.

title: Power-up microheater pulses anneal variable-retention-time defects
idea: Effect: thermally activated defect reconfiguration. VRT cells toggle as a metastable defect switches configuration; TiN microheaters in thermally isolated mats deliver ~us pulses at ~250 C during the JEDEC initialization window (before data exists), biased with a gate field that favours the low-leakage configuration, pruning the VRT population each boot. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): fewer VRT escapes lets the die relax internal refresh ~2x. Risk: which defect state annealing favours is unproven.

title: Bottom-up grown nanowire channels with etch-free sidewalls
idea: Po: chips are grown, not made. Grow single-crystal Si access channels inside the pillar openings by selective epitaxy or tin-catalyzed VLS instead of etching them out of the wafer, so the channel sidewalls carry no plasma-etch damage, the dominant source of trap-assisted leakage in vertical access devices.
why: Facts 3 and 2: a damage-free channel tightens the tail and makes vertical 4F^2 access viable without its usual leakage penalty.

title: KOH-etched {111} sidewall channels: crystal planes replace EUV critical dimensions
idea: K: on (110) silicon, KOH etches {111} planes ~100x slower than others, so DUV-defined trenches self-terminate on atomically flat vertical {111} walls; fins between two such walls are thinned by timed lateral undercut, giving sub-20 nm access channels whose width comes from crystal geometry and etch time, not litho.
why: Atomically smooth {111} interfaces cut interface-trap density and edge-roughness Vt scatter, tightening the leakage tail (fact 3) without EUV (fact 4).

title: Substrate removal by back-side thinning eliminates junction leakage paths
idea: Po: the chip has no floor. After front-end processing, bond the DRAM wafer face-down to a carrier and remove the bulk silicon so access transistors sit in a fully depleted thin body on oxide, deleting the storage-node-to-substrate junction and the substrate holes that feed leakage.
why: Fact 3: junction and substrate-driven tail mechanisms disappear (3-10x tail reduction); the exposed back side also hosts a bias/power plane, freeing periphery area (fact 7).

title: EV power engineer's SiC access tier bonded beneath the capacitors
idea: An EV inverter engineer reaches for 4H-SiC, now mass-produced on 200 mm wafers for cars, including in U.S. fabs. Build high-temperature-activated SiC access MOSFETs first, layer-transfer the 1 um SiC film onto the DRAM wafer, then build capacitors above; SiC's intrinsic carrier density (~1e-9 cm^-3 vs 1e10 for Si) removes thermal generation as a leakage path.
why: Junction and generation leakage drop by many decades, pushing retention from 64 ms toward minutes, so refresh (16-33% of idle power, 10-20% of bandwidth) nearly vanishes; low SiC mobility is acceptable for an access switch.

title: Gated-diode storage amplifies its own charge on read
idea: Replace the capacitor with a planar MOS gated diode. A stored 1 keeps it inverted, so a gate pulse boosts its voltage 3-5x; a stored 0 leaves it depleted with little boost. This fits a 180 nm logic flow.
why: Smaller residual charge still senses correctly, giving a 3-5x longer refresh interval without a high-k capacitor.

title: S-layer protein crystals pattern uniform sub-10-nm access gates
idea: Bacteria coat themselves in self-assembling S-layer protein lattices with 5-15 nm periodicity; recrystallize an S-layer on the BEOL wafer and harden it by sequential infiltration synthesis (ALD alumina at ~90 C) into a perfectly periodic mask that defines access-gate or channel arrays.
why: Molecular periodicity removes the width variation that drives the Vt and leakage tail and replaces 1-2 EUV layers, lowering both tail leakage and capital per wafer.

title: Loadless four-transistor cell held by access-leakage balance
idea: Cross-coupled NMOS drivers with PMOS access devices: in standby, the PMOS off-leakage feeds the high node and outweighs the driver leakage, so the cell latches statically with no refresh (as NEC demonstrated at 180 nm).
why: Refresh-free, ~10 ns access with no capacitor module, buildable in any U.S. legacy logic fab at ~2/3 the area of 6T SRAM.

title: Eliminate refresh with bistable Goto-pair tunnel-diode cell
idea: Make silicon interband tunnel diodes with spin-on dopants and rapid thermal anneal, and series-connect two of them (a Goto pair) at the storage node so their NDR curves create two stable voltages; one access FET writes the node. The cell holds state statically at nA standby current, so refresh is eliminated.
why: Static retention near DRAM density (three devices, vertical diodes) removes refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3); standby current must stay <1 nA/cell.

title: SONOS charge traps repurposed to trim leaky-tail access transistors
idea: SONOS and nanocrystal flash lost on retention and slow programming, neither of which matters if a cell is programmed about once a year. Add a nitride charge-trap layer to the gate stack of the buried-wordline access transistor. After retention test, use hot-carrier pulses to inject electrons into only the ~0.01% of tail transistors, raising their Vt by ~150 mV and pulling them out of the leakage tail.
why: The worst cell sets the refresh interval, so clipping the tail by 1-2 decades allows 4-8x longer refresh at 32-64 Gb. That removes most of the ~46 fJ/bit refresh cost.

title: University cleanroom only: indium-free ALD zinc-tin-oxide access TFTs on MPW CMOS
idea: 10-person constraint: no fab, only a shared university cleanroom. Buy periphery-only CMOS wafers from a 130/180 nm MPW shuttle and post-process the BEOL at <=350 C: ALD ZnSnO channels (no indium or other scarce elements), ALD Al2O3 gates and planar MIM capacitors. This gives access devices with ~1e-20 A/um-class off-current stacked over the logic.
why: Facts 3 and 4 plus resources: demonstrates a refresh-free BEOL memory tile (hours of retention) with no EUV, no indium and no DRAM fab, buildable by ~10 people in ~18 months for niche low-density parts and as a pilot route.

title: Kintsugi artist: in-field electro-thermal anneal heals variable-retention cells
idea: Kintsugi repairs the crack instead of discarding the bowl. When the scrubber finds a variable-retention cell, the controller fires a burst of high-current pulses through that cell's access device to Joule-heat the junction to ~400 C for microseconds, releasing hydrogen from an adjacent hydrogen-rich SiN liner that repassivates the trap.
why: VRT cells set the refresh interval (fact 3) and are remapped or scrapped; in-situ healing shrinks the tail over life, letting refresh periods double or more and recovering yield.

title: Segmented cell plate dips during idle to relax junction field
idea: Box: standard cap x standard access x SA x in-array x Si x one mask that cuts the common cell plate into per-subarray segments. Idle subarrays lower their plate ~0.2-0.3 V, coupling all storage nodes down and reducing reverse bias and gate-edge field on 1-nodes; the plate is restored before activation.
why: GIDL/TAT fall exponentially with field: ~3-5x retention in idle subarrays (fact 3) for one mask.

title: Flip the wafer: backside deep-trench capacitors etched in MEMS fabs
idea: Rearrange front and back: finish access transistors and bitlines on the wafer front in a mature DRAM/logic line, bond to a carrier, thin to ~20-40 um, then use existing 200 mm MEMS-fab DRIE (>=50:1 Bosch etch) to cut deep capacitor trenches from the backside up to each storage node. The capacitor gets the full silicon thickness instead of competing with bitlines for front-side height.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): micron-deep backside trenches give 3-10x Cs at relaxed pitch, and retention scales with it (fact 3); uses idle MEMS/TSV capacity, not EUV.

title: Solar PID-recovery box: nightly reverse-bias de-trapping of access devices
idea: Adapted from the PID-recovery boxes that undo potential-induced degradation in solar parks with a night-time counter-voltage: during idle windows the controller applies reverse gate and well bias to blocks of rows for seconds, emptying charge trapped in access-transistor gate dielectrics and spacers by wordline and hammer stress.
why: Trapped charge raises leakage and causes drift over life (fact 3); routine recovery undoes it, keeping retention near day-one values and delaying replacement.

title: Nanomechanical relay access: an air gap is the off-state
idea: Inverts 'the switch must be a semiconductor': each storage capacitor is isolated by an electrostatically actuated NEMS cantilever relay (Ru- or carbon-coated beam over a ~5 nm air gap) that physically breaks contact, so the OFF state is an open circuit and leakage is only through the capacitor dielectric. Bitlines are equalized before contact closes (cold switching) so contacts survive >10^15 cycles.
why: Removes access leakage entirely (fact 3): retention set by dielectric leakage (seconds to hours), refresh energy and bandwidth tax near zero; abrupt relay switching also allows sub-1 V wordlines instead of ~3 V (fact 10).

title: 2D heterojunction thyristor crossbar: bistable bits without capacitors
idea: IFR: the bit holds itself and needs only two wires. Each crosspoint is a vertical p-n-p-n van der Waals stack (WSe2/MoS2) acting as a thin-film thyristor that latches on or off; a sub-100 pA holding bias keeps '1', '0' draws nothing, and a reverse pulse resets it, so there is no capacitor and no refresh.
why: Constraint: nanometer-thin two-terminal layers allow 8-16 cheap stacked 4F^2 layers, >10x density versus 6F^2, with refresh eliminated if holding current stays below ~100 pA per cell.

title: Chlorine atomic-layer etching thins channels one monolayer at a time
idea: Cl: thin DUV-defined vertical or lateral silicon channels with cyclic Cl2 adsorption plus low-energy ion removal, ~0.5 A per self-limiting cycle, so body-thickness variation across the array falls below ~0.3 nm regardless of the litho that defined the starting shape.
why: Body-thickness variation drives Vt spread and the leakage tail of thin-body access devices (fact 3); atomic-level uniformity substitutes for EUV-level CD control (fact 4).

title: Hyperscaler fleet learning: refresh set from wafer-map telemetry
idea: A hyperscaler runs millions of DIMMs. Log correctable-error and retention telemetry against each die's fab ID (lot, wafer, X-Y) to build a fleet model of retention by wafer position and process lot; new DIMMs get per-bank refresh rates from that model at install, with no slow per-row profiling.
why: Fact 3: ~2-4x average refresh reduction for most dies (edge-of-wafer and weak lots keep 64 ms), sold back to DRAM vendors as a yield-learning data service.

title: Arrhenius canary rows set the die's internal refresh skipping
idea: Effect: thermally activated leakage with known activation energy (~0.6 eV). Each mat holds canary rows with deliberately smaller capacitors that fail at a known fraction of real-cell retention; counters time their decay at actual temperature, and the die skips REF work on real rows whenever canaries prove margin. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Refresh energy and busy time (fact 3): turns the worst-case 32/64 ms guard band into measured margin, -50-80% refresh work at typical temperature.

title: Eliminate shared thermal budgets: transfer-printed silicon nanomembrane access transistors
idea: Fabricate access transistors in SOI nanomembranes with full high-temperature processing, release them, and transfer-print them with an elastomer stamp onto a separately built high-k capacitor backplane. Neither part must survive the other's anneal, so junctions stay pristine and the capacitor gets its crystallization anneal.
why: Decoupling processes avoids anneal-induced leakage degradation and opens heterogeneous stacking toward 3D (fact 2); print alignment limits density.

title: Magnify the domain wall into the switch: LiNbO3 conductive-wall cells
idea: In thin-film LiNbO3 nanofins a write pulse nucleates or erases a charged domain wall across the fin; the wall conducts ~1e6x better than bulk, so the cell reads on/off non-destructively and has no leakage path when the wall is absent. Walls are stable indefinitely at room temperature.
why: Non-volatile, non-destructive read (fact 8), no stored charge to leak; LiNbO3 thin films already run in photonics fabs.

title: Farmer's soil probe: replica-leakage sensor triggers refresh per mat
idea: A farmer irrigates when the soil probe reads dry, not by the calendar. Each 512-row mat gets a 'probe' of 256 minimum-Vt, maximum-GIDL replica access transistors in parallel discharging a 50 fF reference node; a comparator fires that mat's refresh when the replica node crosses the sense limit, so the interval follows real temperature, voltage and aging instead of the 85 C worst case.
why: Refresh (fact 3): servers typically run at 40-60 C, where retention is 4-16x the spec point; a tracking interval cuts refresh energy and lost bandwidth 3-8x for ~0.1% probe area.

title: CRT flyback energy recovery for raster-like refresh sweeps
idea: Revive the television horizontal-deflection flyback circuit, which recycled deflection energy through an LC resonance on every scan line: refresh sweeps rows on a fixed periodic raster, so an on-package resonant LC tank drives the 3 V refresh wordlines and bitline precharge. Most of the CV2 energy returns to the tank at each refresh step instead of being dissipated.
why: Attacks the stuck CV2 energy (fact 10) and refresh's ~46 fJ/bit (fact 3), with 50-70% recovery of wordline and bitline swing energy during refresh.

title: Germanium-rich sacrificial layers set lateral gate length by recess depth
idea: Ge: grow an alternating Si/SiGe superlattice, cut deep slits with DUV, then laterally recess the Ge-rich layers with a self-limiting vapor-HCl atomic-layer etch to a programmed depth; the recess depth, not lithography, sets each tier's lateral access-transistor gate length, and the regrown gate wraps the Si nanosheet.
why: Makes 26+ tier lateral 3D DRAM transistors (fact 2) with nm-controlled gate length from etch chemistry rather than EUV (fact 4); uniform Lg narrows the leakage tail.

title: Heat is the wordline: thermally gated access with 1.5 eV activation
idea: Inverts 'access devices are gated by voltage': put an ionic or deep-trap hopping conductor with ~1.5 eV activation energy in series with each capacitor, effectively insulating at 25 C (retention far beyond hours) while a nanosecond pulse in a row heater line takes it to ~400 C, raising conductance ~10^10x long enough to read or write; cells form 2-terminal crossbar stacks.
why: Two-terminal low-mask crossbar with refresh-free retention, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: heater energy per row access, thermal crosstalk, ~100 ns cycle.

title: Wordline topography shadows tilted halo implant, zero added masks
idea: Box: standard cap x asymmetric access transistor x SA x in-array x Si x high-tilt implant in which the existing wordline/hardmask stack shadows the storage side. Only the bitline side receives the halo dose, so the storage junction stays lightly doped and low-field while short-channel control is kept.
why: Lower storage-junction field cuts TAT/GIDL tail 3-5x (fact 3) without the usual dedicated asymmetric-implant mask.

title: Minify trap density: millisecond laser anneal of storage junction
idea: After the storage-node implant, apply a sub-millisecond laser/flash anneal that heals end-of-range implant defects without diffusing dopants, then high-pressure deuterium sintering to passivate remaining mid-gap traps that create trap-assisted tunneling and variable retention time.
why: Shrinks the <=13 fA tail population ~10x; minimum retention up 2-4x.

title: Package magnet quenches spin-dependent trap-assisted leakage in VRT cells
idea: Effect: spin-dependent recombination/hopping. Trap-assisted tunneling via paramagnetic defect pairs needs spin-pair conversion; a ~0.3-1 T ferrite or SmCo magnet in the package lid polarizes defect and carrier spins, slowing the hop rate of the dominant variable-retention-time trap pairs.
why: Targets the VRT component of the leakage tail (fact 3); honest gain unknown (known effects 0.1-10%), large only if a giant-effect defect class exists; zero die change.

title: Archer's drawn bow: pre-stressed NEMS relay access at 0.2 V
idea: A drawn bow releases great energy at a finger's touch. Each access device is a lateral nanoelectromechanical relay whose beam is built pre-stressed near snap-through (a negative-stiffness bistable flexure), so a 0.2 V gate nudge closes the contact; open, it is an air gap with zero leakage.
why: Zero off-current removes refresh, and a 0.2 V actuation versus a 3 V wordline is ~200x less gate CV^2; key risks are 1e15-cycle contact endurance and ns-scale closing.

title: Particle-detector correlated double sampling: decay-tracking reference cells
idea: Detector front-ends subtract a reference sample taken under identical conditions. Each subarray keeps reference cells written with 1 and 0 at the same moment as the data rows and refreshed with them; the sense reference is set at the midpoint of the decayed reference pair instead of a fixed VBL/2.
why: Fact 3: as stored ones droop the reference follows, so cells stay readable down to much lower residual charge, plausibly a 2-3x longer refresh interval and better temperature tolerance.

title: One-mask BEOL thermistor grid sets refresh per subarray
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x vanadium-oxide thin-film thermistor grid patterned by one added mask above the arrays x per-subarray refresh timers x Si. Each subarray's refresh rate follows its local temperature instead of the hottest die sensor.
why: On-die gradients reach 10-20C in HBM/3D stacks; local rates cut average refresh 30-60% (fact 3) for one mask.

title: Thermoelectric harvester powers key-off self-refresh in hot environments
idea: Worse at 125 C: drain the vehicle battery refreshing DRAM while parked hot. Flip: a Bi2Te3/skutterudite thermoelectric strip between the 125 C module and the chassis harvests 10-50 mW, enough to run self-refresh of the retained partition while the engine bay cools.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) taken off the battery for retained state; enables instant-on without NVM.

title: Cochlear Hopf-bifurcation sense amplifier reads deeply decayed cells
idea: Hair bundles poise near a Hopf bifurcation for huge gain on tiny stimuli; bias each bitline sense amp as a cross-coupled latch with tunable negative resistance held at the edge of oscillation, so a few-mV bitline signal sets its oscillation phase before latching.
why: Cells can lose ~75% of their charge rather than ~50% and still read correctly, so refresh intervals grow ~2-3x, or a smaller capacitor works at today's interval, which also eases the charge wall.

title: DIMM buffer chip takes over refresh with per-row retention map
idea: Rearrange who owns refresh: at OSAT test, profile each die's per-row retention under hot, pattern-stressed conditions and store a compressed weak-row list in a 28 nm buffer/register chip on the DIMM. The buffer intercepts host REF commands, keeps the DRAM out of auto-refresh, and issues RAS-only (ACT/PRE) refreshes at 64 ms only to the ~1% weak rows and at 256 ms+ to the rest.
why: Multi-rate refresh cuts refresh energy and bandwidth ~60-75% (fact 3) on existing commodity DRAM using a trailing-node buffer die; VRT cells need a guard band.

title: Twistor-inspired spiral-ribbon channel for a long, compact access transistor
idea: Borrow Bell Labs' twistor, a helical magnetic tape wound on a wire: grow the access-transistor channel as a helical silicon or oxide-semiconductor ribbon spiralling up a dielectric core inside a 4F2 pillar, with the wordline filling the spiral gap as the gate. Two to three turns give an effective channel length 5-8x the pillar height with no extra footprint.
why: A long channel flattens DIBL and short-channel Vt roll-off, which feed the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3); ~10x lower median leakage and a tighter tail could stretch refresh 4-8x at equal density.

title: Airline heavy-check rotation: drain, heal and return pooled memory live
idea: Adapted from airlines rotating aircraft through heavy checks while the fleet keeps flying: in a CXL memory pool, the fabric manager live-migrates data off a module flagged by retention telemetry, runs a service cycle on it (full retention re-profile, bias recovery, row repair), then returns it, with ~5% spare capacity covering modules in service.
why: Makes in-field retention repair routine with zero downtime (fact 3), so pools can run aggressive relaxed refresh knowing degraded modules are healed before they fail, and modules stay in service longer.

title: Watch-detent Goto pair of tunnel diodes holds each node
idea: Like a watch escapement detent, each storage node is the midpoint of two series tunnel diodes (Goto pair) whose N-shaped I-V curves give two stable voltages. The node self-restores to 0 or 1 at only the diodes' valley current.
why: Zero refresh power: the cell self-latches, so no refresh cycles or sense restores are needed. With pA-class valley currents, total hold power can fall below today's refresh energy.

title: Mitochondrial proton-gradient storage node immune to electron leakage
idea: Mitochondria store energy as a proton gradient across an electron-insulating membrane; store the bit as protons shuttled between two nanometric proton-hosting layers (WO3/HxWO3) through an electron-blocking proton electrolyte, and read it as the conductance of an oxide channel modulated by proton concentration, all deposited near room temperature.
why: The stored state has no electronic leakage path, so retention moves from ms to hours (refresh removed), with ~10-100 ns writes if the electrolyte is a few nm thick; endurance beyond 1e12 is the key risk.

title: Refresh activations double as in-DRAM copy and zeroing
idea: Fuse refresh with RowClone/Ambit-style bulk operations. The controller queues pending page-zeroing, page-copy and scrub-repair work against rows that are due for refresh, and runs each in the same ACT-ACT-PRE that restores the row.
why: Turns the ~46 fJ/bit refresh cost into useful work and absorbs OS zero and copy traffic (5-10% of bandwidth on VM-dense hosts). Net refresh overhead roughly halves.

title: Majority-state inversion plus bitline parking silences idle leakage
idea: Effect: asymmetric leakage (a node at substrate and bitline potential cannot decay). On write, each row gets an internal inversion flag in on-die ECC spare bits chosen so most cells hold the low state; in self-refresh/power-down the bitlines park at 0 V, so those cells see zero drain bias and zero junction bias, and bitlines re-equalize within tXS. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): halves or better the leak-exposed cells per row; with on-die ECC, claims 1.5-2x longer self-refresh interval.

title: Mist-CVD gallium oxide access TFT over stacked capacitor
idea: Box: stacked MIM cap x beta-Ga2O3 (4.8 eV) thin-film access transistor x conventional latch SA x BEOL-over-CMOS x Si wafer x atmospheric mist-CVD at <450C. The wide-bandgap channel suppresses thermal generation so off-current falls toward ~1e-20 A/um, and mist-CVD needs no vacuum tool and no indium.
why: Attacks refresh (fact 3): retention moves from 64 ms toward minutes, cutting refresh energy/bandwidth >100x; In-free, low-capex, US-buildable deposition.

title: Eliminate the solid gate dielectric: air-gap suspended-gate FET
idea: Fabricate a suspended metal gate over the channel on a sacrificial amorphous-Si layer released by XeF2; the gate pulls in electrostatically for access with abrupt switching and springs back to a large air gap in hold, deepening the off state and removing gate-oxide traps. Unlike a contact relay, current still flows through a semiconductor channel.
why: Steep switching cuts wordline voltage and leakage together (facts 3, 10); sacrificial MEMS release is routine in university fabs; stiction and speed are risks.

title: PERC solar trick: negative-charge alumina liners silence storage-junction surface leakage
idea: PERC solar cells keep minority carriers off the rear surface with ALD Al2O3 carrying ~10^13 cm^-2 negative fixed charge. Line the storage-node contact sidewall and STI edge, where the n+ junction meets a surface, with the same charged Al2O3 so holes accumulate in the p-well surface and the depletion region (and its interface-trap generation) is pushed off the surface.
why: Perimeter/surface generation is a large part of the junction-leakage tail (fact 3); field-effect passivation cut solar surface recombination ~10x, so 3-5x lower tail leakage and 2-4x longer refresh interval is plausible.

title: Time-release capsule: buried hydrogen reservoir re-passivates traps over product life
idea: Extended-release drugs meter an active ingredient for years from an embedded reservoir. Embed a hydrogen-rich silicon nitride layer, sealed above by a dense diffusion barrier, a few hundred nm below the cell array so it slowly releases hydrogen at 85 C operation and keeps re-passivating dangling bonds created by hot-carrier and VRT activity.
why: The retention tail drifts with aging and in-field VRT (fact 3); a self-replenishing passivant keeps the tail tight for 10 years and removes the ~2x end-of-life refresh guardband.

title: Plumber's pressure equalization: well bias idles the storage junction
idea: A plumber knows no pressure difference means no leak. During idle, the bank's p-well is raised ~0.4 V and the cell plate shifted to preserve stored levels, so the storage-node junction sees near-zero reverse bias and the field-enhanced trap-assisted tunneling behind the leakage tail collapses; both are restored a few ns before any activation.
why: The weak-cell tail is trap-assisted tunneling and GIDL, exponentially field-dependent: cutting peak junction field ~40% can raise tail retention 4-10x and cut idle/self-refresh power, today 16-33% of idle.

title: No-conduction-path rule: NEMS relay as the cell access switch
idea: Self-imposed limit: the off state may contain no solid conduction path at all. Replace the access MOSFET with a vertical nano-electromechanical relay sitting on the capacitor: a 10 nm gap with a low-adhesion Ru- or Pt-coated contact that the wordline pulls in electrostatically. When open, the vacuum/air gap leaks less than an attoamp, so retention is set only by capacitor dielectric leakage.
why: Fact 3: removes the <=13 fA subthreshold, GIDL and junction tail entirely. Refresh goes from 64 ms to minutes or hours, and the 16-33% idle refresh power nearly vanishes. Risk: contact endurance (~1e15 cycles needed) and ns switching at nanoscale.

title: Float-glass style liquid-gallium printing of atomically thin Ga2O3 channels
idea: As float glass forms on molten tin, kiss the wafer against a liquid Ga/In alloy. Its self-limiting 1.5-3 nm oxide skin transfers at room temperature as a crystalline wide-gap 2D channel for BEOL access transistors.
why: Eg ~4.8 eV in an atomically thin channel could push off-current below 1e-21 A per cell (beyond IGZO). It is BEOL-stackable for 3D with no epitaxy tool, aiming for >100x less refresh.

title: Refresh hides in compute bubbles: pull-in synchronized to AI kernel phases
idea: 10-person constraint: only the scheduler is ours. A runtime hook signals the memory controller when a compute-bound phase starts (e.g. a high-arithmetic-intensity GEMM tile). The controller pulls in up to the JEDEC-allowed 8 pending refreshes during that bubble and postpones refresh during bandwidth-bound phases.
why: Fact 3: refresh's 10-20% bandwidth tax moves into windows when DRAM bandwidth would sit idle, recovering most of it for memory-bound kernels via driver and firmware.

title: Neighbor wordlines driven deeper negative while a row is open
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x SA x sub-wordline drivers given a second negative rail selected for rows N+-1 during row N activation x in-array x Si x zero masks. The extra ~-0.3 V on adjacent wordlines cancels coupling and passing-gate effects that transiently open neighbor access transistors.
why: Cuts activation-induced leakage that erodes neighbor retention and drives row hammer (facts 3, 9): ~2x retention under heavy traffic, higher hammer threshold.

title: MEMS bulk-micromachining: TMAH crystallographic etch makes atomically smooth access pillars
idea: MEMS fabs carve mirror-flat silicon walls along slow-etching crystal planes with alkaline TMAH, no plasma. Define vertical access pillars with an amorphous-carbon hard mask opened in O2 plasma, rough-etch with Cl2/HBr, then finish sidewalls in dilute TMAH so channel faces terminate on crystal planes, replacing SF6/fluorocarbon etch and its damage and polymer residue.
why: Plasma-damaged, rough sidewalls set Dit in 4F2 vertical transistors; crystallographic faces could cut Dit 3-10x and tighten Vt spread, shrinking the leakage tail (fact 3) while dropping PFAS-class etch gases.

title: Plywood cross-grain laminated channels break grain-boundary leakage paths
idea: Build the poly channel of 3D/BEOL access transistors as 3-5 ultrathin plies with rotated texture and amorphous seams between them, so grain boundaries never line up through the film. This copies the way plywood crosses its grain to stop through-splits.
why: Off-state tail in poly-Si or poly-oxide channels is set by the worst percolating GB path. Misaligned plies could cut the tail ~10x while on-current still flows along the plies.

title: Borrow power-MOSFET field plate to flatten storage-node field
idea: Substitute the bare gate-drain overlap with a grounded buried field plate, as used in power LDMOS: a thin TiN shield in the isolation next to the storage contact, tied to ground. It spreads the lateral field so the peak field at the overlap drops ~20-30%.
why: GIDL is exponential in peak field, so tail cells see ~10x less GIDL and the wordline can be biased more negative without a GIDL penalty: 4-8x longer refresh interval.

title: Nanoelectromechanical contact in series with each access transistor
idea: A monolithic BEOL TiN or CNT cantilever relay sits between the access transistor and the storage node. The same wordline field pulls it in, and it springs open during retention to leave an air gap.
why: The off-state leakage path is a vacuum or air gap, so retention is limited only by capacitor-dielectric leakage and refresh is eliminated for most data. Nanosecond closure and contact wear are unproven.

title: Low-self-discharge battery separator: crested tunnel barrier in storage-node contact
idea: Low-self-discharge NiMH cells won with a separator that blocks slow parasitic currents while passing charge current. Insert a crested (triangular-profile SiO2/Si3N4/SiO2-type) tunnel barrier in the storage contact: at write/read bias the crest collapses and current flows, while at the few hundred mV seen in retention tunneling falls exponentially, starving the off-transistor leakage path.
why: Adds a >10^4 current nonlinearity between ~1 V and ~0.3 V in series with the subthreshold path (fact 3); could raise retention ~100x while keeping 10-20 ns access if the barrier stays thin.

title: Kovio printed silicon diode pairs as two-way crosspoint access
idea: Kovio's printed-silicon RFID died because printed tags had to undercut cheap silicon chips. Use its cyclopentasilane ink, crystallized by flash lamp, to print two opposing p-i-n diodes per cell, one to a write-1 line and one to a write-0 line. When idle, the storage node is isolated by two reverse-biased diodes, giving a transistor-free crosspoint 2D1C cell.
why: Printable access with no transistor, with leakage set by reverse diode current, and the cells can be stacked in printed tiers. Memory's value per m2 justifies the cost of printed silicon where RFID's did not.

title: Day-old bread pricing: discounted refresh-disabled perishable-memory cloud SKU
idea: Cloud providers sell refresh-disabled DRAM capacity at a discount, the way bakeries sell day-old bread. It comes with a retention SLA (e.g., data valid for 200 ms after its last write) for batch shuffles, caches and inference scratch. Hypervisors map it to unrefreshed banks.
why: Zero refresh power on that capacity. It creates a market price signal that turns refresh-free operation into extra usable supply during the shortage.

title: Replace transistor with two-terminal punch-through selector: cross-point DRAM
idea: Substitute the 3-terminal access transistor with a 2-terminal n+/p-/n+ punch-through (or back-to-back Schottky) selector stacked on an MIM capacitor at every wordline/bitline crossing (1S1C). Idle lines sit at mid-level so each selector sees near-zero bias, and writes use V/2 half-select.
why: A stackable 4F^2 cross-point cell with no lateral transistor (the 3D DRAM blocker): denser per layer, with many layers. Retention needs a selector nonlinearity of >1e9 between V and V/2.

title: Interface dipole sets access Vt so channel doping can drop
idea: Effect: interfacial dipole at the high-k/SiO2 boundary. An Al2O3 dipole monolayer shifts the buried-wordline gate's effective work function by +0.2-0.3 V, letting channel boron doping fall ~3x; lower doping lowers the peak storage-junction field, and field-enhanced trap-assisted tunneling drops ~10x. DDR/HBM pins, commands and timings stay unchanged.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ~3-4x internal refresh relaxation from a single film change.

title: Magnify mechanical inertia: bistable buckled nanobeam bit
idea: Store each bit as the up/down state of a pre-compressed, snap-through-bistable 100 nm SiN nanobeam; electrodes above and below snap it in ns and its position is read capacitively by a gain transistor. No charge is retained, so nothing leaks, and elastic flexing has no oxide-breakdown wear mechanism.
why: Non-volatile, zero refresh, abundant materials; elastic endurance targeted >1e15.

title: Eliminate the one-size retention spec: per-die retention descriptor standard
idea: Propose a JEDEC extension in which each die stores its measured retention distribution (per bank, per temperature) in an on-die fuse table and the host sets tREFI per bank from it; validated dies advertise 128-512 ms classes. The single worst-case 64 ms contract disappears.
why: Most dies retain far longer than spec; per-die refresh rates cut refresh power and bandwidth loss 2-8x industry-wide with zero fab capital.

title: Monolayer WSe2 channel wrapped around the capacitor pillar sidewall
idea: Thermal generation scales with depleted semiconductor volume times n_i. A 0.7 nm monolayer has almost no volume and a gap of ~1.6-2 eV. Grow MOCVD WSe2 or MoS2 conformally (<500 C) on the outer sidewall of the vertical storage pillar with a ring wordline. The result is a gate-all-around vertical access device with no silicon body and a 4F^2 footprint.
why: Leakage drops ~1e6 from n_i and ~10x from volume, removing the junction and TAT tail sources (fact 3). It also gives a vertical, stackable cell (fact 2) with no lateral transistor.

title: LCD active-matrix backplane repurposed as bulk dynamic memory
idea: An LCD pixel is already a 1T1C DRAM cell refreshed at 60 Hz. Depreciated Gen-2/3 a-Si or LTPS lines (2-4 um rules) could pattern huge TFT-capacitor arrays with on-glass sense amps, and very wide rows offset the microsecond row time.
why: Attacks capital intensity, since those lines cost ~1/100 per area, and avoids EUV entirely. Density and latency are far below DRAM, so it fits only as a wide, slower bulk tier.

title: Ultra-short local bitlines trade sense margin into retention
idea: Worse: hang 1,024 cells on a bitline so the signal is tiny and any leakage kills the bit. Flip: hierarchical bitlines with 32-cell local segments and a local gain transistor raise the charge-transfer ratio from ~0.2 to ~0.8, so a cell can lose 3x more charge before failure.
why: Retention about 3x, refresh down about 65%, and the same trick relaxes the Cs wall (fact 1).

title: Line-tunneling TFET access device exploits DRAM's tiny on-current need
idea: Worse: use a thermionic MOSFET whose off-state is set by kT. Flip: DRAM writes need only ~5-10 uA for ~10 ns, so use a vertical line-tunneling Si/SiGe TFET whose only injection path is band-to-band tunneling, giving sub-aA off-current when the gate is low.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) 100x+ lower; refresh interval in the seconds range at 85 C.

title: Per-row canary cells request refresh when they fade
idea: IFR: memory refreshes only when it is about to forget. Add 2-4 canary cells per row written at ~70% charge, polled by a tiny comparator in the sub-wordline driver during low-power checks; a row is refreshed only when its canaries flip.
why: Fact 3: retention varies 10-100x by row and temperature; canary-driven refresh cuts refresh operations 4-10x and tracks VRT and temperature in situ.

title: Locksmith combination-lock access: resonant-tunneling barrier opens only at key bias
idea: Replace the gated transistor with a double-barrier resonant-tunneling stack (e.g., AlN/GaN wells) between bitline and storage well. Charge passes only when the bitline bias aligns the quantized level, like a key cut to one combination. Off-resonance, thick wide-gap barriers block flow.
why: Zero refresh: off-resonance transmission and thermionic leakage over ~2 eV barriers give retention of years, and energy-selective access needs no gate oxide or junction.

title: HP SAIL single-stamp imprint patterns roll-to-roll oxide access arrays
idea: HP's self-aligned imprint lithography (spun out as Phicot) died chasing large display backplanes, where web stretch ruined overlay. Pattern every layer of an oxide-TFT access array on a web with one multi-height imprint stamp, etched back level by level, so the layers stay self-aligned whatever the foil distortion. Target small memory tiles that can absorb defects through redundancy.
why: Mask-free, EUV-free access devices with oxide-class leakage (<=1e-18 A) at roll-to-roll cost, for a refresh-light memory-foil tier. Capital intensity drops by orders of magnitude.

title: OS-driven TRIM for DRAM: never refresh dead rows
idea: IFR: only living data is maintained. A new JEDEC command, like SSD TRIM, lets the OS and hypervisor declare row ranges free (freed pages, ballooned guest memory); the device refresh counter skips them until the next write.
why: Fact 3: servers often hold 20-50% unallocated or dead DRAM, so refresh energy and bandwidth fall proportionally through a spec and firmware change.

title: Pump-less VPP: refresh wordlines fed from a board GaN rail
idea: Worse: generate the 3 V wordline supply with on-die charge pumps at ~30% efficiency. Flip: deliver VPP from a high-efficiency GaN point-of-load converter on the module through dedicated balls, removing the pumps and their area.
why: Refresh and activation energy (facts 3, 10) down ~25-30%; frees periphery area (fact 7).

title: Milestone prize for capacitorless 4F^2 cell meeting DRAM spec
idea: Po: the government bans capacitors. Fund a U.S. prize with staged payouts: $50M for a capacitorless 4F^2 cell holding 64 ms at 85 C on 300 mm wafers, $200M for a 1 Gb array at 1e15 endurance made in a domestic fab, with IP licensed to all U.S. makers.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: pulls many capacitorless paths forward in parallel for a few hundred million dollars instead of a $15B fab.
